entities.name: Joseph-Emmanuel de La Trémoille
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Joseph-Emmanuel de La Trémoille (d. 1720), a scion of the powerful House of La Trémoille, served as a French cardinal, Archbishop of Cambrai, and a pivotal diplomatic figure in Rome for two decades during the tumultuous early 18th century. His career spanned the final years of Louis XIV's reign and the Regency, positioning him at the nexus of ecclesiastical power and Bourbon foreign policy, particularly concerning the Papacy and the critical negotiations surrounding the War of the Spanish Succession. He was instrumental in shaping France's relationship with the Holy See during a period marked by shifting European alliances and the assertion of Gallican liberties against papal authority.

Appointed Archbishop of Cambrai in 1697, La Trémoille rarely resided in his archdiocese, dedicating his energies instead to his diplomatic mission as French ambassador to the Holy See from 1700. Elevated to cardinal in 1706 by Pope Clement XI, he became a central intermediary between the French Crown and the Vatican. His diplomatic efforts focused on maintaining French influence in Italy, managing the complex issue of Gallicanism, and navigating the Papacy's often conflicting allegiances during the War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714), where papal neutrality was perpetually challenged by Bourbon and Habsburg interests. He played a direct role in the conclave of 1700, which elected Clement XI, and later in the negotiations that followed the Treaty of Utrecht.

Joseph-Emmanuel de La Trémoille (1659-06-28, France) was a French Cardinal.

De La Trémoille played a pivotal role in the Catholic Church during the Early Modern era. As a cardinal, he participated in several high-level diplomatic missions to European monarchies and contributed significantly to the Church's efforts to maintain its influence in Western Europe.

One of his most notable achievements was his involvement in the development of the Code of Canon Law, which would go on to shape Catholic doctrine for centuries to come. Additionally, de La Trémoille collaborated with other prominent clergy and theologians to promote the spread of Catholicism through education and missionary work.

Despite facing challenges from Protestant reformers and secularizing trends in 18th-century Europe, de La Trémoille remained a respected figure within the Church.

The legacy of Joseph-Emmanuel de La Trémoille can be seen in the enduring influence of Catholicism on European society and politics, as well as his contributions to the development of canon law.

"A true servant of the Lord," de La Trémoille was remembered by contemporaries for his piety and unwavering commitment to the Church's mission.
